text:
# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–14 (Complete – Updated 113)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Summer of fourth year in Mirecombe hill farms. Earlier: Spring of fourth year with Seena Orlwood drowned in flood, others at Mirecombe (Pebin Wexwood, Maric Lindson, Rozek Hollwood, Halan Hollwood, Isbin Hollwood, Orvie, Nynelle Stenworth, Seena Hollett, Brenelle and Orvie Hollett, Thidrek Corrett, Feten Lindner, Old Maric, Ilena Orlwood, Orrine, Staveton). Winter of third year with frost on hedges. Evening at Brighton following Dobbin's arrival. Fine brilliant moonlight night of May. Army ordered to Belgium; embarkation completed two days after Mrs. O'Dowd's party. Transports proceeded under convoy to Ostend with band playing "God Save the King." Amelia and Jos proceeded to Ramsgate for passage to Ostend. **All now in Belgium in happy season (spring transitioning to summer); Rawdon and Rebecca arrived in Brussels; military festival, churches, galleries, rides, opera ongoing; greatest event of history (Waterloo campaign) imminent; French have crossed frontier; great news stirring; campaign opening summer of 1815; Famous ball given by noble Duchess at Brussels on 15 June 1815 (historical event); all Brussels in state of excitement; English ladies struggled intensely for tickets.**
- **Primary Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street counting-house, Slaughters' hotel, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers on Lombard Street, Long Acre with herald), Brighton (George-Amelia honeymoon, Rawdon-Rebecca residence, Ship Inn, beach), Mirecombe (various residents), Wilhaven (harbor town), Chatham (embarkation point, 150th regiment mess, Mrs. O'Dowd's apartments), Harwich, Fulham (Mrs. Sedley's house, Mr. and Mrs. Clapp, Miss Flannigan), Ramsgate, Ostend, Brussels (Hotel de Ville, flower-market, Park, Hotel du Parc—Rawdon and Rebecca's residence with General Tufto, opera-house, restaurateur's establishment, general's party venue, Marshy aux Flures flower market, famous ball venue), Belgium (flat, flourishing country with green fields, quiet cities, chaussees, canal-boats, rich pastures, pleasant villages, old chateaux; Queen's Crawley noted as riding-instruction location; crowded with well-to-do English travellers; Highlanders billeted in Flemish farm-houses). Bryngate market town mentioned. Road conditions: ruts and puddles after thaw; frost silvered hedges; rain threatened but held off.

## Main Characters

**Captain William Dobbin** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Earlier Actions**: Arrived Brighton via Slaughters' hotel; witnessed Stubble's tears; dined with officers. At Ship Inn: assumed jovial manner hiding feelings upon seeing Amelia; made clumsy compliments. In George's room: delivered disinheritance letter; George erupted; Dobbin offered financial support, promised not to forget godson; George forgave him. Evening dinner: described Belgium fetes and fashion; flushed red when Rebecca announced intention to go to Belgium, objected about danger, became confused and silent. At Cavendish Square Hotel: attempted remonstrance against extravagance; George dismissed concerns. Walked home musing. At Chatham: wore shells on frockcoat, crimson sash and sabre; paced street in expectation; presented military appearance. Recognized Amelia upon arrival. Never spoke to Amelia during Mrs. O'Dowd's party; took Jos home (maudlin state); handed Amelia into carriage as she departed; she rebuked him smilingly for ignoring her; loitered smoking cigar afterward watching lights from George's windows; did not return to quarters until almost morning. Bought piano for Amelia's father's house at Fulham.
- **In Belgium**: "In a rage" at behaviour of Lady Blanche Thistlewood and Countess of Bareacres toward Amelia at George's dinner party. Accompanied Jos and Amelia on carriage drives in Brussels Park. Encountered Rawdon and Rebecca in park; exchanged faintest specimens of politeness with Rawdon. When Rebecca kissed fingers playfully toward carriage at opera, Dobbin shrieked with laughter and ran from box; when Mrs. O'Dowd mistook Rebecca's hand-kissing for herself and returned salute, Dobbin shrieked out of box again. Does not draw out Mrs. O'Dowd as George does. At opera: Rebecca leaned on his arm when returning to her box (choosing him over George to "stay and talk to his dearest, best, little Amelia"). Expressed disapproval of Rebecca to George after opera, calling her "a humbug" who "writhes and twists about like a snake" and was "acting at the General." George dismissed his concerns. Few days after opera: remonstrated with George about giving up play, promised to Dobbin for "any time these hundred years"; George evaded by asking when Dobbin would give up sermonising. **Friend of General commanding the division; obtained invitation to famous Brussels ball through this connection; invited to display similar invitation to Mrs. Osborne (made Jos envious, George wonder). At the ball: only person except Dobbin who came to disturb Amelia's unhappy thoughts as she sat unnoticed in corner; brought her refreshments and sat beside her; when Amelia clinging to him (calling him by Christian name as George did), told him she was unwell and asked him to take her home; he went away with her quickly through crowds; her lodgings were hard by.**
- **Internal Conflict**: Deeply troubled by guilt over hastening marriage; feels his unendurable suspense drove him to crush uncertainty; considers himself traitor to both father and son. Secret adoration of Amelia is his "greatest privilege and hope of life"; privately resolved he would not have let her go to Belgium if married to her. Knows Amelia considers him plain, awkward, ungainly; acquiesces humbly. Now avoided by George in public and regiment; visits Osborne house without advantage of meeting George; painful and unavailing talk spared between them.
- **Reputation**: "Greatly respected in the regiment, as the best officer and the cleverest man in it"

**George Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Status**: Married Amelia late April without father's consent; disinherited by lawyer letter (determination "final and irrevocable"). Receives £2,000 in 4 percent annuities and £100/year widow's allowance for Amelia.
- **Financial Activity**: Lost £140 to Rawdon Crawley at cards; gave substantial payment from bank-notes and bill on agents. Hotel bill and card losses nearly drained purse. Obtained £2,000 cheque from Hulker and Bullock bankers. Fred Bullock turned deadly colour at bankers. At Chatham: sent Amelia to her mother with strict orders and carte blanche to purchase everything requisite for Mrs. George Osborne's fashion. Paid with cheques "with the splendour of a lord." At Brussels ball: commanded new dresses and ornaments of all sorts for Amelia.
- **In Belgium**: Ashamed of regiment company and resolved to exchange into better regiment soon and get wife away from "damned vulgar women" (Amelia herself remains unaffected and unembarrassed). Takes wife to nightly jaunts and junkets; quite pleased with himself; swears becoming domestic character. Sight of great company of lords, ladies, and fashionable persons fills his truly British soul with intense delight. Had honour of dancing with Lady Blanche Thistlewood, Lord Bareacres' daughter; bustled for ices and refreshments; pushed and squeezed for carriage; bragged about Countess at home. Called upon ladies next day; rode by their side in Park; asked their party to great dinner at restaurateur's; wild with exultation when they agreed. Spent great deal of money on this festival entertainment. Mrs. Sedley in London mightily pleased. Purchased horse for private riding; accompanied Jos and Amelia on carriage drives in Brussels Park. Delighted to see Rawdon leaning over carriage talking to Amelia; met Rawdon's cordial greeting with more than corresponding warmth. Invited Rawdon and Rebecca to dinner, mentioning Lord Bareacres, Countess, and Lady Blanche dined previously to establish fashion credentials. Told wife Rebecca's arrival is comfort as she will be friend and allow him to "get rid of this damn'd Irishwoman" (Mrs. O'Dowd). Desires to distinguish himself prodigiously in campaign so father relents. Reflects "the world was before him" and luck might change at cards. **At opera: consulted with herald in Long Acre fifteen years prior and picked the L------ arms out of the peerage when he set up his carriage; claimed "We bear the same arms" to General Tufto; Rebecca left his box to visit Amelia's, giving George "the queerest, knowingest look" when together, a look suggesting manipulation ("Don't you see the state of affairs, and what a fool I'm making of him?") though George did not perceive it. After opera: Dobbin criticized Rebecca; George defended her as "the nicest little woman in England," saying Dobbin "ain't a man of the world" and praising her shoulder and ability to "talk over Tufto in no time." Few days after opera: told Dobbin "we play low; I won last night" and suggested Crawley does not cheat; plays repeatedly with Crawley now. General Tufto dines abroad almost constantly; George always welcome in Crawley's apartments (very close to General's) in hotel.**
- **Character Assessment**: Has "firm conviction in his own mind that he was a woman-killer and destined to conquer"; believes himself "rather free about women" and has stated this smiling and nodding knowingly to mess-table comrades, who respect him for this prowess. Carrying on "desperate flirtation with Mrs. Crawley"; rides with her whenever she is free; pretends regimental business to Amelia (by which falsehood she is not in the least deceived); consigns his wife to solitude or her brother's society and passes evenings in Crawleys' company; loses money to Rawdon and flatters himself wife is "dying of love for him." **At Brussels ball: obtained card for Captain and Mrs. Osborne through interest of Lord Bareacres, as set-off for dinner at restaurateur's; circumstance greatly elated him. Danced with Rebecca twice or thrice; left Amelia on bench after looking about for Lady Blanche (who cut him); later came at Rebecca's request to get her scarf and flowers (done twenty times before in course of last few days); was angry twice or thrice at finding wife up on his return from parties he frequented. Not angry with himself about woman's expense or with women themselves—"if a pretty woman WILL throw herself in your way, why, what can a fellow do?" Next to conquering in war, conquering in love has been source of pride time out of mind amongst men in Vanity Fair.**
- **Relationship Status**: Nearly had first quarrel with Amelia over her unwillingness to visit Rebecca and high and mighty manner; George scolded Amelia violently; she did not reply but was bashful and awkward on second visit.

**Amelia Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Earlier Actions**: Troubled by Rebecca's wit; misgivings about Rebecca; tormented by guilt about forcing marriage and causing disinheritance. Face cleared reading disinheritance letter. Cried with "greatest spirit" determination to accompany George to Belgium. Rose early; packed trunks with "greatest alacrity" while George lay in bed. Made "little disappointed curtsey" when George declined accompanying her to Fulham. Mother clasped her to heart with "all maternal eagerness and affection," ran out weeping; old Mr. Clapp alarmed in shirt-sleeves; Irish servant-lass rushed up smiling "God bless you." Upstairs to little room: sank into chair; fell to thinking over past week; reflected on Rebecca's "twinkling green eyes and baleful smile"; indulged in selfish brooding and listless melancholy; thought with terror of funereal damask pavilion at grand hotel; knelt by bedside seeking spiritual consolation. When tea announced, came downstairs "a great deal more cheerful"; kissed father and mother; talked to old gentleman making him more merry than many a day; sat at piano (purchased by Dobbin) and sang all his favourite old songs; praised tea and marmalade arrangement; finding herself so by determining to make everybody else happy; was sound asleep in pavilion; woke with smile when George arrived from theatre. Bustling about from milliner to linen-draper completing outfit with great taste and elegant discernment; Mrs. Sedley sincerely happy for first time since misfortunes. At Mrs. O'Dowd's Party: Recognized lady as one George often laughed about. Grasped Amelia's hand very warmly. Being quiet, good-natured, and not too handsome, made agreeable impression until gentlemen arrived, who all admired her so sisters began to find fault. Had "little triumph" which flushed spirits and made eyes sparkle. Resolved: "I will make all his friends welcome. I will love all as I love him. I will always try and be gay and good-humoured and make his home happy." Adopted by regiment with acclamation.
- **In Belgium**: A natural and unaffected person with none of artificial shamefacedness; only amused by Mrs. O'Dowd's honest eccentricities, not in least ashamed of her company. Letters home to mother filled with delight and gratitude. Husband bade her buy laces, millinery, jewels, gimcracks; he was kindest, best, most generous of men. Thought about her husband and how best to show her love for him amid great topics of world. Every day during happy time brought novelty and amusement. At general's party given for George's regiment division: Countess of Bareacres would not answer when spoken to; Lady Blanche stared with eye-glass; Amelia wrote most piteous accounts home; ladies carefully excluded her from conversation. In Brussels Park: Rebecca acknowledged Amelia with gracious nod, smile, and playful finger-kissing; Amelia received this with her usual composure. At opera: gentle eyes fixed anxiously on Rebecca and George's pair; when Rebecca entered her box, Amelia flew to her friend with affectionate rapture, embracing her dearest friend in presence of whole house (full view of General's glass). Received Rebecca kindly despite Rebecca's evident manipulations. Overpowered by flash, dazzle, and fashionable talk of her worldly rival. When George visited Crawley's quarters with Amelia, she displayed evident unwillingness and high and mighty manner toward Rebecca; George scolded her violently; she did not say one single word in reply but with George's eye upon her and Rebecca scanning her, was more bashful and awkward on second visit than first. Neither lady rallied beyond Mrs. O'Dowd's timely observation. **Now not quite six weeks married. Aware George carrying on flirtation with Rebecca; does not say much or plague him with jealousy but becomes unhappy and pines over it miserably in secret. George does not know she is not suspicious (though all his acquaintance are perfectly aware). At Brussels ball: did not know a single soul; after George placed her on bench and left her to her own cogitations, her thoughts were not of the pleasantest; sat quite unnoticed in corner except when Rawdon came with clumsy conversation and Dobbin brought refreshments. Alarmed by Rebecca telling her George would go on playing. Witnessing Rebecca's request to George for scarf and flowers scene proved "quite too much for her"; suddenly clinging to Dobbin called him by Christian name (as George did), telling him she was unwell and begging him to take her home; he went away with her quickly through crowds; her lodgings were hard by; did not know she called him William. Did not sleep although din, clatter, and galloping of horsemen were incessant; never heard these noises, having quite other disturbances to keep her awake.**

**Mrs. Major Peggy O'Dowd** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- One of five sisters and eleven children of noble house of Glenmalony; ordered cousin Mick O'Dowd to marry her when about thirty-three after trying nine seasons at Dublin and two at Bath and Cheltenham. Mick obeyed and carried her to West Indies. At Mrs. O'Dowd's Party: Sent Amelia triangular billet on pink paper sealed with dove and olive branch; received her warmly with great vivacity; told of her birth and pedigree; expressed intention that Glorvina would have suited George; determined to take Amelia as sister; assured they would agree. Dispatched Ensign Simple to Colonel Tavish about Jos. Gossiped at tea-time about George's reformed rake status and Amelia's position as wife. Inquired about Mrs. Kirk's evangelical questions; presented penny books. Assisted Jos in learning military names with great assiduity.
- **In Belgium**: Traveling with Amelia and Jos as one of "most entertaining" companions; continually prattles about Ballinasloe canal-boats, Dublin cattle (father's gold medal heifer), comparison of markets, Ballinafad, Glenmalony stables, claret drunk there. Remarked about flowers and magolias at Glenmalony. Cock's plume in hat and very large repeater on stomach which she rings on all occasions, narrating it presented by her fawther as she stept into carriage after marriage; these ornaments and other peculiarities give excruciating agonies to Captain Osborne when wives in contact; Amelia only amused by honest lady's eccentricities. Accompanied Jos and Amelia on carriage drives in Brussels Park. At opera: wore splendid Irish diamonds and Cairngorms outshining all decorations; tossed about clattering fan with splendid complacency; remarked Brussels opera-house not so fine as Fishamble Street theatre Dublin; French music not equal to native country melodies. When Rebecca performed hand-kissing to Amelia in opera box, Mrs. O'Dowd mistakenly took compliment to herself and returned gracious smile, sending Dobbin shrieking from box. Rebecca admired her large Cairngorm brooch and superb Irish diamonds, wouldn't believe they were not from Golconda direct. Presence still excruciated Osborne but she goes upon all parties of pleasure; never entered her thought but they must be charmed with her company. Made timely observation when neither lady rallied after Rebecca's brilliant apparition ("Why didn't you BOY one?" regarding bouquets); became silent and subdued, scarcely said a word more about Glenmalony all evening, silenced by Rebecca's flash and dazzle. **Panting to be asked for Brussels ball tickets; strove in vain to procure them.**

**Major Mick O'Dowd** [MINOR CHARACTER]
- Served sovereign in every quarter of world; paid for every step by acts of daring and gallantry. Most modest, silent, sheep-faced, meek of little men; obedient to wife as if tay-boy. At mess-table sits silently and drinks great deal; when full of liquor, reels silently home. Speaks only to agree with everybody on every point; passes through life in perfect ease and good-humour. Never heated temper in hottest suns of India; never shaken by Walcheren ague. Walked up to battery with same indifference as to dinner-table; dined on horse-flesh and turtle with equal relish.

**Jos Sedley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Earlier Actions**: Arrived Chatham in fine carriage with Amelia. Recognized friendly countenance of Captain Dobbin. Attended Mrs. O'Dowd's party in maudlin state; told tiger-hunt story with great effect. Dobbin and Captain Porter took him home to hotel. Agreed to escort Amelia and Mrs. O'Dowd abroad. Ceased shaving upper lip upon agreeing. Followed parades and drills with great assiduity at Chatham; listened with utmost attention to "brother officers." Received excellent assistance from Mrs. O'Dowd in military studies. Made appearance in braided frock-coat and duck trousers, foraging cap with smart gold band. Had carriage; informed everybody on board Lovely Rose confidentially he was joining Duke of Wellington's army; folks mistook him for commissary-general or government courier. Courage prodigious; cried "Boney attack us!"; assured "poor Emmy" of no danger; explained allied military superiority.
- **In Belgium**: Interposed about curry and rice at Dumdum during Belgium journey; owned with sigh that for good streaky beef mingled with fat and lean, there was no country like England (despite Mrs. O'Dowd's patriotic assertions about Irish beef). Hired pair of horses for open carriage in Brussels; made tolerable figure in drives about Brussels Park with smart London vehicle. Accompanied Amelia on carriage drives; more at ease when great man (General Tufto with Rebecca) departed. Referenced Battle of Salamanca; proclaimed "The jungle's the school for a general"; reminded Mrs. O'Dowd he danced same evening with Miss Cutler, daughter of Cutler of Artillery (devilish fine girl) at Dumdum. George urged him to cut off his moustache and remove infernal frogs from his coat. At opera: eating ice; Rebecca admired Jos with "kindliest greeting" and bustled, chattered, turned and twisted, smiled upon one and smirked on another, all in full view of jealous opera-glass opposite. **At Brussels ball: panting to be asked with Mrs. O'Dowd; strove in vain to procure tickets (others more lucky); made Jos envious when Dobbin displayed invitation obtained through General commanding division.**

**John Osborne (Old Mr. Osborne)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Wealthy merchant; George's father; savage, determined man. Upon learning George married Amelia, erupted in fury. Retreated to study; locked door; retrieved mahogany escritoire; examined George's documents with "curses quivering on livid lips" and "horrid hatred and disappointment"; marked, docketed, catalogued with dates. Commissioned lawyer to draft letter stating determination "final and irrevocable." George ceases to be family member; Money expended in minority exceeds entitlement; Osborne waives all claim upon George's estate. In London, news how son is entertaining peers and peeresses actually came to Osborne's ears in the City.

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Secretly married to Rawdon; heavily indebted. All reconciliation attempts with Miss Crawley permanently rebuffed; Miss Crawley refused Rebecca and Rawdon; sent Rawdon to lawyer with negative outcome; disparaged Rawdon's appearance and habits. Successfully reconciled with Miss Briggs on beach through letter-writing campaign; Miss Crawley recognized Rebecca's composition and concluded "that little serpent of a governess who rules him." Monetary scheme executed: sent crumpled note to Rawdon requesting money from "Cupid" (George); Rawdon extracted considerable payment in bank-notes and bill on agents. Rebecca remarked: "A comfortable inn in Brighton is better than a spunging-house in Chancery Lane"; noted Jos and Captain Cupid are better companions than sheriff's officers. Packed chief valuables and sent them off under care of George's servant on coach to London.
- **In Belgium**: Now in Brussels with Rawdon and General Tufto (lodging at Hotel du Parc). Encountered Osborne party in Brussels Park riding on beautiful little Arab in prettiest and tightest riding-habit, riding to perfection (acquired art at Queen's Crawley from Baronet, Mr. Pitt, and Rawdon). Accompanied by General Tufto amid troop of greatest persons in Brussels. Acknowledged Amelia graciously with nod, smile, and playful finger-kissing. When Rawdon asked General who fat officer in gold-laced cap was, replied he was officer in East Indian service (referring to Jos). Rawdon shook hands with Amelia and spoke warmly to Jos. At opera: performed hand-kissing toward Amelia's box; caught Amelia's eye; clapped hands together and held out both hands to George when he entered her box, charmed to see him. General Tufto's presence in box noted; he stared at George with sulky scowl when George entered. Rebecca then left box with George, giving him "the queerest, knowingest look" suggesting manipulation of General Tufto ("Don't you see the state of affairs, and what a fool I'm making of him?") though George did not perceive it. Returned to her box leaning on Captain Dobbin's arm (choosing him over George to leave Amelia with George—"he must stay and talk to his dearest, best, little Amelia"). During her time in Amelia's box, bustled, chattered, turned and twisted, smiled upon one, smirked on another, admired Mrs. O'Dowd's Cairngorm brooch and Irish diamonds, all in full view of jealous opera-glass (General's glass) opposite. During ballet time skipped back to her own box leaning on Dobbin's arm. After opera, General Tufto cursed "so deep, that no compositor would venture to print them"; curses came from heart; human heart capable of generating such lust and fury, rage and hatred. General was jealous and angry about Rebecca and George together. Osborne and Crawley repeatedly together now; George always welcome in their apartments (very close to General's) in hotel. George not perceiving Rebecca's manipulation. When Amelia and George visited Rawdon and Rebecca's quarters, Amelia displayed evident unwillingness and high and mighty manner toward Rebecca; nearly caused first George-Amelia quarrel; George scolded Amelia violently; Amelia bashful and awkward on second visit. Rebecca remarked to George: thought Amelia was jealous of her at Brighton; now supposes Amelia is scandalised because Rawdon, Rebecca, and General live together; questioned how they could live at all without friend to share expenses; asked if George supposed "Rawdon is not big enough to take care of my honour"; claimed she was "very much obliged to Emmy, very"; also revealed General Tufto was jealous of George and ready to "eat me for going with you to visit that foolish little wife of yours" ("as if I care a pin for either of you"); pert toss of head; inviting George to dinner; General (the dragon) dines with Commander-in-Chief; great news stirring—French have crossed frontier; will have quiet dinner. **At Brussels ball: invited; was of course invited as became friends of General commanding cavalry brigade. During ball: George danced with Rebecca twice or thrice; Amelia scarcely knew how many times. Made request to George for her scarf and flowers (done twenty times before in last few days); this proved too much for Amelia.**

**Rawdon Crawley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Secretly married to Rebecca; heavily indebted. Extracted considerable payment from George in bank-notes and bill on agents; lost £140 to George at cards. Met Miss Crawley when she took air in chair; she held out couple of fingers; Rawdon turned red as scarlet with rapture and confusion. Miss Crawley subsequently disparaged his appearance, character, and drinking. Visited Miss Crawley's lawyer in Gray's Inn Square; "came back furious" to Rebecca.
- **In Belgium**: Now in Brussels lodging at Hotel du Parc with Rebecca and General Tufto. Encountered Osborne party in park; rode out of ranks of his company and came up and shook hands heartily with Amelia and spoke warmly to Jos ("Well, old boy, how are you?"); stared at Mrs. O'Dowd's face and black cock's feathers until she thought she made conquest of him. Later sent message to George at opera inviting him to dinner Tuesday when General dines out; also invited George and others to "come speedily" and asked George to "make Sedley cut off his moustache." Rawdon said "Hm, as you please" when George expressed intention to pay respects to Rebecca alone, looking very glum; two young officers of fashion on general's staff exchanged knowing glances. Repeatedly together with George now; George always welcome in their apartments. **Lets Osborne come and go with entire good humour; understood perfectly well with Rebecca (though never absolutely conspired in so many words) that one cajoled the young gentleman whilst other won his money at cards; winning money to Osborne while flattering himself wife dying of love for him.**

**General Tufto** [MINOR CHARACTER]
- Military officer in Brussels with considerable status. Lodging at Hotel du Parc with Rawdon and Rebecca. Attended army gatherings and social events. Rebecca riding in Park "by the side of the gallant General Tufto." Asked Rawdon who "fat officer was in the gold-laced cap" when saw Jos. Dines out almost constantly; Tuesday mentioned as occasion when General away dining with Commander-in-Chief. **At opera: stared at George with "sulky scowl" when George entered Rebecca's box; disengaged eye working round in Rebecca's direction, shooting out bloodshot glances at her and George; when Rebecca left box with George, General gave low utterance to curses "so deep, that no compositor would venture to print them"; curses came from heart; was jealous and angry; ready to "eat me for going with you to visit that foolish little wife of yours" (Amelia). General capable of generating such lust and fury, rage and hatred.**

## Critical Facts and Status

- **MILITARY CAMPAIGN - BELGIUM, IMMINENT COMBAT**: Regiment departed Chatham two days after Mrs. O'Dowd's party; transports proceeded under convoy to Ostend with band playing "God Save the King." All now in Belgium enjoying "happy time" with military festival, churches, galleries, rides, opera; English bugles wake soldiers each morning; at nightfall British fife and drum; **greatest event of history (Waterloo campaign) imminent; French have crossed frontier; great news stirring; Commander-in-Chief dining (campaign about to commence).**
- **GEORGE-AMELIA MARRIAGE - ESTABLISHED BUT DEEPLY FRACTURED**: Married late April; disinheritance "final and irrevocable"; obtained £2,000 cheque; George ashamed of regiment company but resolved to exchange soon. Amelia emotionally stable, grateful, loves George deeply, received triumph at Mrs. O'Dowd's party. Both in Belgium; George takes her to nightly jaunts and junkets. **Nearly had first quarrel over Amelia's evident unwillingness to visit Rebecca and high and mighty manner toward her; George scolded Amelia violently; Amelia silent but bashful and awkward on second visit. Now not quite six weeks married. George carrying on "desperate flirtation" with Rebecca; rides with her whenever free; pretends regimental business to Amelia (by which falsehood she is not in least deceived); consigns wife to solitude or Jos's society; passes evenings in Crawleys' company; loses money to Rawdon; flatters himself wife "dying of love for him." Does not know Amelia is not suspicious (all his acquaintance perfectly aware). Amelia does not say much or plague him with jealousy but becomes unhappy and pines miserably in secret. At Brussels ball: George obtained invitation; left Amelia on bench unnoticed in corner; danced with Rebecca twice or thrice; came at Rebecca's request for scarf and flowers (done twenty times before in last few days); Amelia found this "quite too much"; called Dobbin by Christian name, begged him to take her home; did not sleep that night; heard only disturbances to her heart.**
- **REBECCA-RAWDON-GENERAL TUFTO TRIANGLE - VOLATILE MANIPULATION AT PEAK**: Both Rawdon and Rebecca in Brussels lodging at Hotel du Parc with General Tufto; financially precarious situation ongoing. Rebecca established in fashionable circles, riding in Park with General, attending social events. Rawdon in contact with George and other officers. **General Tufto deeply jealous of George and Rebecca's interactions; cursed with intense rage and fury after opera when Rebecca left box with George. Rebecca manipulating both men—keeping General jealous while cultivating George's attention; George responding warmly and playing cards repeatedly with Rawdon; tensions present (officers exchanged knowing glances). Rawdon and Rebecca understand each other perfectly well: one cajoled young gentleman while other won money at cards. George not perceiving manipulation. General dines abroad almost constantly (away from Hotel du Parc). George always welcome in Rawdon and Rebecca's apartments. Rebecca invited George to dinner while General dines with Commander-in-Chief. French frontier crossed; campaign imminent. Both Rawdon and Rebecca invited to Brussels ball.**
